description: TheAstro is a Türkiye-based team of students and developers passionate about space exploration, science, and technology. Our goal is to build an intuitive, data-driven astronaut health monitoring system for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. We combine software development, data visualization, and creative problem-solving. We welcome motivated teammates with skills in research, UI/UX design, data science, space biology, and communication.
summary:
AstroTwin is a crew health monitoring web app for long-duration missions, built for a crew on the way to Mars. On a Mars mission the crew can be about 11 minutes away from Earth one way, so they cannot wait for a doctor's answer. AstroTwin acts as an onboard "flight surgeon assistant": it scores each astronaut's health continuously, explains what changed, and tells the crew what to do now.

Its key idea is "three normals". Every reading is compared with Earth reference ranges, the astronaut's own personal baseline from the first flight days, and the expected adaptation curve for spaceflight. In our simulated hidden-decline scenario, this flags a problem 15 days earlier than a simple Earth threshold.

AstroTwin combines live NASA space weather data (DONKI, GOES protons) and JPL Horizons signal delay with NASA Human Research Program knowledge of the five spaceflight hazards. It writes delay-aware SBAR reports to Mission Control and lets the crew control what routine reports share. The scoring is rule-based and transparent. AI only explains it and never makes the medical decision.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

AstroTwin is a health "digital twin" for each crew member on a simulated Mars transit. It answers three questions every day: Is this astronaut OK? What changed? What should the crew do right now, without waiting for Earth?

HOW IT WORKS

1. Collect – simulated vitals (heart rate, blood pressure, SpO2, body temperature, sleep, activity, radiation dose) plus a short daily check-in based on measures NASA uses with astronauts. [Daily Check'i bitirdiysen ekle:] The daily check covers five areas: sleep and alertness (Karolinska Sleepiness Scale), mind and focus (a short reaction test inspired by the PVT-B "Reaction Self-Test" used on the ISS), mood and stress, physical symptoms, and crew connection.

2. Score – a deterministic rules engine compares every value with three normals: Earth reference ranges, the astronaut's personal baseline (flight days 1–14), and the expected spaceflight adaptation curve. Compound rules catch risks that only appear together, for example a solar particle event combined with poor sleep, or headache plus high cabin CO2. A mismatch rule flags when someone reports feeling fine but their data disagrees, because astronauts may not notice their own cognitive decline.

3. Act – each crew member gets a clear Nominal / Watch / Alert status, a "why this matters" explanation, and concrete next steps (rest, recheck, shelter during a radiation event, tell the flight surgeon).

4. Report – AstroTwin writes SBAR reports for Mission Control in three tiers (Routine, Anomaly, Critical) and calculates the real Earth–Mars signal delay from JPL Horizons, so the crew knows when an answer can arrive. Crew members decide what routine reports share. Critical alerts are always sent.

LIVE NASA DATA

NASA DONKI solar particle events, CMEs and notifications; NOAA SWPC GOES proton flux; and JPL Horizons Earth–Mars distance (about 11 minutes one-way delay in our scenario). A built-in replay of the May 2024 solar storm (GLE74) shows how AstroTwin reacts to a real event. A Data & Sources page inside the app separates live data, NASA research references and simulated data.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

- Earlier detection: in the simulated hidden-decline scenario, personal baselines flag a problem on day 21 instead of day 36.

- Crew autonomy when Earth is minutes away.

- Transparent, testable logic: scores come from rules, not a black box. A language model (optional, Gemini) only narrates the results in plain language and cannot change any score.

- Privacy by design for small, isolated crews.

- Same approach on Earth: Antarctic stations, submarines, offshore workers, remote clinics.

TOOLS

React + TypeScript, installable offline-first PWA, Node.js/Express proxy that keeps API keys server-side, Docker, [65] automated unit tests for the scoring engine. APIs: NASA DONKI (api.nasa.gov), NOAA SWPC, JPL Horizons, optional Google Gemini.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

NASA HRP's five hazards (radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, hostile closed environment) and the fact that hazards compound. Communication delay. Psychological safety and privacy. Not giving medical diagnoses or medication doses. Clearly labeling all simulated crew data.

LINKS

Live app: https://twin.theastro.us

Source code: https://github.com/zulfumirza/astrotwin

LIMITATIONS

All crew vitals are simulated. This is a research prototype, not a medical device.
